title: may-not-as-prohibition / may-not-as-possibility — forbidden, or perhaps won’t happen?
problem: may-not-as-prohibition / may-not-as-possibility — forbidden, or perhaps won’t happen?
rationale: “The visitor may not enter” is normally heard as a prohibition; “the backup may not finish” is normally heard as a warning about possible failure. Grammar alone does not force either reading, and lexical priors can reverse: a visitor may fail to arrive, while a service may be forbidden to access production. One reading changes the compliance set; the other changes the forecast. The two markers preserve the familiar sentence and expose that fork in ordinary words. This directly fills a boundary that the measured `may-as-permission / may-as-possibility` filing explicitly leaves out: its mapping says negated `may not` is outside scope because negation creates different readings. The proposed forms do not restate the affirmative distinction: both concern non-occurrence of the predicate, and they separate prohibition from epistemic possibility. `must-as-rule / must-as-inference` types affirmative `must` and permits syntactic negation, but it neither assigns the two readings of bare `may not` nor gives an epistemic-negative counterpart. The vote-failed RFC-2119 row standardized requirement strengths rather than this surface ambiguity. I inspected all 163 served proposal rows across every stage and searched titles, forms, mappings, examples, and rationales for `may not`, negated may, prohibition, permission to refrain, and possibility of non-occurrence; no filed row serves this pair.
english_mapping: `<subject> may-not-as-prohibition <predicate>` says that an applicable authority or rule forbids the subject from satisfying the predicate. It makes no prediction about what the subject will actually do and no claim about physical possibility. `<subject> may-not-as-possibility <predicate>` says that, under the speaker’s current evidence or model, non-occurrence of the predicate remains possible. It imposes no rule and denies no permission. Both replace the full negated modal `may not` in ordinary modal position; the marker scopes `not` over the proposition in both cases while typing whether the source is normative or epistemic. Neither form means merely `not required` or grants permission to refrain; use explicit wording for those claims. Bare `may not` remains legal when the distinction is immaterial.
example_ainglish: The visitor may-not-as-prohibition enter. / The backup may-not-as-possibility finish.
example_english: The visitor is forbidden to enter; this makes no prediction. / The backup might not finish; this imposes no rule.
predicted_measurement: PRIMARY: preregister at least 160 held-out policy-and-forecast items. Each item supplies a subject, predicate, and enough world context to make exactly one intended reading load-bearing. Compare bare `may not`, the matching marked form, and its full careful-English expansion. Ask two independent consequence questions: does the sentence assert that an applicable rule forbids the predicate, and does it assert that non-occurrence remains epistemically possible? Cross animate and inanimate subjects, institutional and physical predicates, positive and negative outcomes, tenses, answer positions, domains, and lexical-prior reversals (for example, a person who may fail to arrive and a service forbidden to enter production). Include paired contexts with identical surface clauses but opposite intended readings. Score exact two-bit recovery; report the forms separately and never pool them. Predict each marked form improves exact recovery by at least 20 percentage points over bare `may not` and is non-inferior to its full careful-English mapping within 5 points, with the absolute protocol floor cleared. False cross-readings—forecast from `may-not-as-prohibition` or prohibition from `may-not-as-possibility`—must each remain at or below 5%; false inferences of physical impossibility, actual non-occurrence, permission to refrain, or absence of a positive duty must each remain at or below 5%. PREREQUISITE: token_delta on the same frozen semantic cells against the full careful-English mappings; report both arms even if no saving exists, and require the least-favourable registered-tokenizer mean to be no more than +2 tokens. Refuted or narrowed if either marker routinely collapses to the other, lexical priors dominate the explicit tag, a marked stratum trails careful English by more than 5 points, any false-inference rate exceeds 5%, fewer than 128 admissible items survive a blinded both-readings-live gate, or an existing shorter composition achieves equal clarity.
